questions.q: What is the common real-world security mistake this lesson describes?
options: Writing a wide-open NSG/security group rule during setup, planning to tighten it later, and that cleanup never actually happening
Forgetting to create any NSG or security group at all
Using too many narrow rules instead of one broad rule
Deploying NSGs before the subnets they attach to exist
questions.explain: The widely-open 'temporary' rule, written to stop fighting connectivity errors during setup, routinely never gets tightened back down afterward.

questions.q: What does a security rule scoped to source '*' and port '*' actually allow?
options: Any protocol, on any port, from any source
Only HTTPS traffic from the internet
Only traffic from inside the same subnet
Nothing — a wildcard rule is automatically ignored
questions.explain: '*' (equivalent to 0.0.0.0/0) means any source is allowed, combined with any port and any protocol — the widest possible rule.

questions.q: What do Azure NSGs and AWS security groups do with inbound traffic that no rule explicitly allows?
options: They deny it by default
They allow it by default unless explicitly blocked
They forward it to a manual approval queue
They allow it only during business hours
questions.explain: Both NSGs and security groups default to denying inbound traffic unless a rule specifically permits it.

questions.q: Why does this lesson give each subnet (web, app, data) its own NSG/security group instead of one shared rule set?
options: So each tier only allows the specific access it actually needs, like the data tier being reachable only from the app tier
Because Azure and AWS require a separate NSG per subnet by law
Because shared NSGs are more expensive to run
Because a single NSG can only attach to one subnet technically
questions.explain: Per-tier rules enforce least privilege: the data tier should only accept traffic from the app tier, not from the web tier or the internet.

questions.q: What is the practical effort difference between writing a least-privilege rule and a wide-open rule?
options: Essentially none — it's the same number of commands, just with the real source and port filled in instead of a wildcard
A least-privilege rule requires an entirely separate deployment pipeline
A least-privilege rule can only be written after the wide-open rule is removed first
Writing a least-privilege rule takes significantly more commands
questions.explain: The az network nsg rule create and aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress calls are identical in structure either way — only the values change.
